text:
Strengthening coordination among institutions responsible for protecting Nigerians from violence has taken centre stage in a review of the implementation of the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015, as government agencies and civil society organisations met in Abuja to validate the draft 2025 Implementation Report.
The review, coordinated by the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), is funded by the European Union through the Rule of Law and Anti-Corruption (RoLAC) Programme, implemented by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA).
The stakeholder meeting marked the culmination of five months of peer review, during which institutions and organisations involved in implementing the Act examined their respective efforts, shared experiences and assessed how their work could be better coordinated.
The process recognises that the effectiveness of the VAPP Act depends partly on how well the institutions responsible for its implementation work together, account for their actions and respond to the protection needs of vulnerable persons.
The need for stronger implementation is reflected in national findings. The 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey reported that 19 per cent of women aged 15–49 had experienced physical violence since age 15, while 5 per cent had experienced sexual violence.
Public awareness of the VAPP Act also remains limited. A 2025 survey by Invictus Africa, which covered 11,574 respondents across 35 states, found that more than half of respondents had never heard of the VAPP Act. Only 29 per cent of those who were aware of the law said they understood its provisions well.
Passed in 2015, the VAPP Act provides a legal framework for addressing different forms of violence, including rape, domestic violence and harmful traditional practices. However, the existence of legislation does not automatically guarantee that survivors can report abuse, obtain protection or secure justice. These outcomes depend on how effectively the institutions responsible for implementation work together.
The annual review process has been part of efforts to monitor the law’s implementation over several years. NAPTIP presented the first implementation report, covering 2020, in December 2021. Reports for subsequent years have continued to document the work of implementing institutions and the challenges they face.
The latest review seeks to deepen this process by encouraging institutions to assess their own contributions alongside those of other actors, rather than treating implementation as the responsibility of individual agencies.
Speaking at the meeting, Mrs Maureen Lance-Onyeiwu, Project Manager of the RoLAC Programme, said the European Union’s consistent support had helped sustain the VAPP Act as an instrument of accountability for government and civil society organisations working to advance its provisions. She said the review was intended to build a common understanding of what had been achieved, the challenges institutions continued to face and the priorities requiring attention.
According to her, producing the report was only one part of the exercise. The broader objective was to translate institutional reflection into practical improvements in the responsibilities stakeholders have under the Act.
Also speaking, Mrs Chidinma ThankGod said the annual implementation report serves as an accountability and monitoring tool for assessing progress, identifying gaps and strengthening efforts to prevent and respond to violence against persons.
She explained that the validation of the 2025 report was important to ensure that the experiences of implementing institutions were properly documented and that recommendations were grounded in evidence.
The review meeting also brought together members of HIMAT and SPARC, with Professor Fatima Adamu facilitating the examination of the draft report and guiding discussions on feedback and proposed revisions.
For survivors of violence, the effectiveness of the Act depends on whether the institutions mandated to protect them can translate its provisions into meaningful responses, access to justice and appropriate support.
The report, following the validation process and subsequent finalisation, is expected to provide a basis for improved planning, institutional coordination and follow-up on the implementation of the Act.
